\chapter{Hablais --- the Form Spain Keeps}
\label{ch:spanish-hablais}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can recognise the vosotros form and say where it is used.}

vos + otros, added in Spain to keep the plural apart from a singular vos the Americas kept instead.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[habláis]{habláis — the form Spain keeps}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-hablais}



\begin{quote}
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}you all speak\textquotedblright{} to a group in Mexico? (\emph{Ustedes hablan}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a second plural you}]
In Spain, addressing a group of \textbf{friends} uses a different word and a different verb form:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vosotros habláis} — \emph{you all speak}, informally.
\end{quote}

\textbf{vosotros} — \emph{you all}, familiar. Its ending is \textbf{-áis}, and it is the last of the six.

This is not an ornament. In Spain it is the ordinary, everyday way to speak to more than one friend, and a Spaniard hears \emph{ustedes} to a group of friends as oddly formal — roughly as an English speaker hears \emph{sir} from someone they know well.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
You met \textbf{vos} long ago: Latin's \emph{plural} you, which drifted into the singular across much of the Americas.

That drift left Spain with a problem. If \emph{vos} was being used for one polite person, what was left for an actual group? Spaniards added a word to disambiguate: \textbf{vos + otros}, \textquotedblleft{}you \textbf{others}\textquotedblright{} — hence \emph{vosotros}, and its feminine \emph{vosotras}.

The Americas never needed the repair, because \emph{ustedes} had already taken the plural job. So the split is not a difference of taste. \textbf{Two regions solved the same problem in two different ways}, and both solutions are still in use.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{What you owe this form.} Recognition, at minimum — you will meet it in every book, film and song from Spain. Produce it if you are learning for Spain; otherwise \emph{ustedes} will carry you anywhere.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU HEAR: \textquotedblleft{}habláis\textquotedblright{}{]} $\to$ a Spaniard, talking to friends.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}ustedes hablan\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}vosotros habláis\textquotedblright{} — the same sentence, two continents
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{vosotros} built from? (\textbf{Vos + otros} — \textquotedblleft{}you others\textquotedblright{}.) Why did Spain need it and the Americas not? (Because \emph{vos} had drifted singular in the Americas, where \emph{ustedes} already covered the plural.) Which will carry you anywhere? (\textbf{Ustedes}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
